title: CRT & discrete logs
syllabusUnit: Unit III: Chinese Remainder Theorem & Discrete Logarithms
covers: Chinese Remainder Theorem, exponentiation, discrete logarithm
learningGoals: You will be able to solve simultaneous modular equations using the Chinese Remainder Theorem.
You will be able to calculate fast modular exponentiation using Square-and-Multiply.
You will be able to explain the Discrete Logarithm Problem.

lessonCards.title: The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)
lessonCards.analogy: Three clocks running at different speeds (mod 3, mod 5, mod 7) all align at a unique hour.
lessonCards.coreConcept: If moduli m1, m2, ..., mk are pairwise coprime, a system of congruences x = a_i (mod m_i) has a single unique solution modulo M = m1 * m2 * ... * mk.
lessonCards.example: CRT speeds up RSA private key decryption by up to 4x by splitting calculations modulo p and modulo q.

lessonCards.title: Square-and-Multiply Exponentiation
lessonCards.analogy: Instead of multiplying 2 thirty times, square 2 five times: 2 -> 4 -> 16 -> 256.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Fast exponentiation computes a^b mod n in O(log b) steps by scanning exponent bits: square on every bit, multiply if the bit is 1.
lessonCards.example: Computes 3^1000 mod 77 in milliseconds instead of billions of operations.

lessonCards.title: The Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP)
lessonCards.analogy: Spinning a roulette wheel 50 clicks is easy; looking at the ball and guessing the clicks is hard.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Given base g, modulus p, and result y = g^x mod p, finding x is the Discrete Logarithm Problem. There is no known fast classical shortcut.
lessonCards.example: Diffie-Hellman and ElGamal rely directly on the hardness of DLP.

questions.prompt: What does the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) guarantee when moduli m1, m2, ..., mk are pairwise coprime?
options: There exists a unique solution x modulo the product M = m1 * m2 * ... * mk
questions.explanation: CRT guarantees an exact, unique simultaneous solution modulo the product M = m1 * m2 * ... * mk.
wrongExplanations: Correct! A unique solution exists modulo the product of coprime moduli.
Solutions are guaranteed to exist.
Moduli remain positive integers.
The solution depends on the system remainders.
questions.realWorldExample: Sunzi Suanjing (Sun Tzu's Mathematical Classic) described this theorem in 3rd century AD China.

questions.prompt: How does RSA hardware decryption benefit from using the Chinese Remainder Theorem?
options: It splits 2048-bit exponentiation into two faster 1024-bit operations modulo p and q (approx. 4x speedup)
It eliminates the need for prime numbers
It doubles the key size to 4096 bits automatically
questions.explanation: Since modular multiplication scales quadratically O(n^2), two half-sized operations execute four times faster than one full-sized operation.
wrongExplanations: Correct! CRT provides a dramatic 4x speedup in RSA private key signing and decryption.
Primes p and q are strictly required to use CRT.
Key size is unchanged.
Encryption remains separate.
questions.realWorldExample: Almost all production cryptographic hardware (smart cards, HSMs) uses RSA-CRT decryption.

questions.prompt: What is the 'Discrete Logarithm Problem' in a finite cyclic group Z_p*?
options: Given g, p, and y = g^x mod p, find secret integer exponent x
Divide two prime numbers by zero
questions.explanation: While computing y = g^x mod p is fast via square-and-multiply, computing x = log_g(y) mod p is computationally intractable for large primes.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Finding the exponent x is the Discrete Logarithm Problem.
Square roots are quadratic residues, not DLP.
Division by zero is undefined.
Basic multiplication is trivial.
questions.realWorldExample: Diffie-Hellman key exchange security depends entirely on the hardness of discrete logs.

questions.prompt: How many multiplications does the Square-and-Multiply algorithm require to compute a^b mod n, where b has k bits?
questions.explanation: For each bit in exponent b, one square is performed, and at most one multiply if the bit is 1, totaling at most 2 * log2(b) operations.
wrongExplanations: Correct! O(log b) complexity makes huge 2048-bit powers computationally practical.
Linear b multiplications would freeze computers on large exponents.
b^2 is exponential in bit length.
Multiplications are required.
questions.realWorldExample: RSA decryption a^d mod n computes 2048-bit exponents in under 2 milliseconds.

questions.prompt: What is a 'primitive root' or 'generator' g of a prime modulus p?
options: A number whose powers g^1, g^2, ..., g^(p-1) generate all integers from 1 to p-1 modulo p
A number that divides p evenly
questions.explanation: A generator g produces the entire multiplicative group of units modulo p without missing any non-zero element.
wrongExplanations: Correct! g generates every non-zero remainder modulo p.
Primes have no divisors other than 1 and p.
Generators are integers, not irrational roots.
Generators in Z_p* are positive integers.
questions.realWorldExample: In Diffie-Hellman, generator g = 2 or g = 5 is commonly selected.

questions.prompt: Why must the moduli in the Chinese Remainder Theorem be pairwise coprime (gcd(m_i, m_j) = 1)?
options: To guarantee that modular inverses exist during the reconstruction step
Because prime numbers are illegal otherwise
So the numbers add up to 100
questions.explanation: If moduli share common factors, modular inverses cannot be computed and conflicting congruence constraints may arise.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Pairwise coprimality ensures unique modular inverses exist for each base M_i.
Moduli do not need to be prime, only pairwise coprime.
Sum has no mathematical requirement.
Division succeeds cleanly.
questions.realWorldExample: CRT is widely used in error-correcting codes, digital signal processing, and cryptography.

ashRecap: CRT lets us solve big problems by breaking them into smaller clock pieces. Discrete logs are easy to spin forward, but impossible to run backward!
